meta.blurb: Marta is fifty-seven when she cannot rise from the lawn without help. With her neighbour Sam, a physiotherapist, she learns how muscles, bones, balance and friends can stay strong for decades, one small step at a time.
meta.bible: Marta: a warm, stubborn woman of fifty-seven who wants to keep up with her grandson. Leo: her grandson, five years old, full of energy. Sam: her neighbour, a Physiotherapist in his sixties, calm, practical and funny. Walter: Marta's friend with arthritis and a heart condition. Joy: Marta's friend who starts a walking group. They live in a small town with a Park, a Library and a hill called Beacon Hill. Marta's Story runs from one spring to the next summer. Key facts: Muscle and strength tend to decline gradually with age, but much of the loss is linked to using muscles less, and training helps at any age. The World Health Organization advises adults to do at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, muscle-strengthening on two or more days, and (for older adults) balance practice on about three days. Key terms: Aerobic, Strength, Balance, Protein, Calcium, Osteoporosis, Sit-to-stand, Tai chi, Physiotherapist. Voice: kind, practical and encouraging, never scary, hedged where evidence is uncertain, no invented numbers or studies. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

B1B2: Marta, who is fifty-seven, has been playing on the lawn with her grandson Leo. When it is time for lunch, she cannot stand up again without pulling herself up on a garden chair.
Marta tells her neighbour Sam, a physiotherapist, what happened on the lawn. He smiles kindly and says that many people notice this around her age, and that it can often be improved.
Sam explains that muscle and strength tend to fall slowly as we get older, often beginning in middle age. The change is gradual, which is why most people only notice it years later.
However, Sam says that age is only part of the story. Much of the loss is linked to using our muscles less, and that is something we can change.

Studies of older adults, some of them in their eighties and nineties, have found that strength training can make muscles stronger. The body keeps its ability to adapt, so it is never too late to start.
Sam tells Marta to see her doctor first if she has a heart problem, chest pain, dizziness or a long illness. She decides to book a check-up anyway, just to be safe.

Sam explains that a healthy body needs four kinds of movement: aerobic activity, strength work, balance practice and gentle stretching. Each one protects something different from the others, so a good week includes all four.

The World Health Organization suggests at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, along with muscle work on two days. That sounds like a lot, but it can be spread across the whole week, and Sam says anything is better than nothing.

Marta does not begin with a big plan, because Sam has warned her that big plans are the first thing to fail. She simply walks around the block for ten minutes after breakfast, and that is enough for the first week.
Sam gives her a simple test for a moderate pace. If she can talk but cannot sing a song, she is working at about the right level.
After two weeks of daily walks, Marta feels a little brighter and she is sleeping better. Her legs are not magic yet, but she has found that she wants to go out.
Sam suggests linking the new habit to something Marta already does every day, such as drinking her morning tea. When one action follows the other, she no longer has to decide whether to go.
Regular aerobic activity trains the heart just as it trains the legs. Over weeks, the heart can pump more blood with each beat, so everyday tasks feel easier.
Sam warns that sitting still for hours is hard on the body, even for people who exercise. He suggests standing up and moving for a minute or two every half hour.
Strong muscles do far more than lift heavy bags in the shop. They help us climb stairs and keep our balance, and they also help the body to manage blood sugar.
The first strength exercise is a simple one called the sit-to-stand. Marta sits on a firm chair, folds her arms, stands up slowly and sits down again, and she does it five times.
Next comes the wall push-up, which is much easier than a push-up on the floor. Marta stands an arm's length from the wall, bends her elbows to bring her chest closer and then pushes herself back.

The third exercise is the calf raise, which she can do while the kettle boils. Holding the kitchen counter for safety, Marta rises slowly onto her toes and lowers herself again to strengthen her lower legs.
Sam hands her a long elastic resistance band, which costs very little. She can also use tins of food or a bag of shopping when she wants something heavier.
To keep getting stronger, she must ask her muscles for a little more as time passes. This idea is called progressive overload, and it can mean one more repetition or slightly more weight.
Sam tells her that muscles get stronger during rest, not during the exercise itself. She should leave at least a day between hard strength sessions for the same muscles.
A mild muscle ache a day or two after exercise is normal, Sam says. Sharp or sudden pain, or pain in a joint, is different, and it is a signal to stop and get advice.
Sam tells her that good form matters more than heavy weight. She should move slowly, breathe out during the hard part and never hold her breath.
Sam explains that muscles are built from protein, and older muscles seem to respond less well to it. Many people over fifty may therefore benefit from eating a little more of it.
Sam suggests spreading protein across the day instead of eating most of it at dinner. People with kidney disease, however, should ask their doctor before changing how much protein they eat.
Sam warns that crash diets can take away muscle as well as fat. If she wants to lose weight, he says, slow and steady is kinder to her muscles.

Sam explains that bones are living tissue that is always being rebuilt. As people age, especially after the menopause in women, bones can become thinner and break more easily, a condition called osteoporosis.

Bones respond to load, just as muscles do, so they become stronger when they are asked to carry weight. Walking, climbing stairs and strength exercises give them a reason to stay strong, whereas swimming and cycling do less for the bones.

Bones need calcium, which is found in dairy foods, tinned fish with bones and some green vegetables. They also need vitamin D, which the skin makes in sunlight, and a doctor can say whether a supplement is needed.
In many countries, about one in four people over sixty-five falls each year. Balance can be trained, and training it lowers the chance of a fall.
The simplest balance exercise is standing on one leg beside the counter, with a hand ready to catch her. Marta does it every night while she brushes her teeth.
Next she tries walking heel to toe along a line of tape on the floor, as if on a tightrope. Sam also recommends tai chi, a slow Chinese exercise that studies suggest may lower the risk of falling.
Sam walks through her house and points out hazards. A loose rug, a dark staircase and slippery slippers can all cause a fall, and each is easy to fix.
Marta finishes each walk with a few minutes of gentle stretching. She holds each stretch for about half a minute, never bouncing and never pushing into pain.
Marta worries about her sore knees, because she thinks that exercise will make them worse. Sam says that gentle movement usually helps stiff joints, because it keeps the muscles around them strong.
One week her knee is sore, so Marta swaps her walk for a ride on an exercise bike. Low-impact activities like cycling and swimming keep her fit without jarring the joint.
Sam reminds her that the body repairs itself during sleep. Most adults need about seven to nine hours, and poor sleep makes exercise harder and recovery slower.
Smoking harms the heart, lungs and bones, and stopping helps at any age. Heavy drinking is also hard on the body, so Sam suggests keeping alcohol modest.
Marta asks her friend Joy to join her walks. When someone is waiting for you at the gate, it is much harder to stay in bed.
Research links strong friendships with better health, and loneliness with poorer health. Joy starts a Saturday walking group on Beacon Hill, and within a month ten people are coming.
Regular exercise can lift mood and ease worry for many people. It is not a replacement for professional help, however, if someone feels low for a long time.

Some studies suggest that regular activity may help memory and thinking as we age. The evidence is not yet certain, but it is promising, and exercise has so many other benefits that it makes sense anyway.
Marta catches a heavy cold and misses two weeks of exercise. When she feels well again, she restarts at a lower level instead of picking up where she left off.
To measure progress, Marta times herself for thirty seconds and counts how many times she can stand up from a chair. Her number slowly rises, and that is more useful than any number on a scale.
On a warm summer day, Marta plays on the lawn with Leo again. When lunch is called, she stands up without any help and he does not even notice.
Marta realises that strength was never about big muscles. It is about independence, and about being able to do the things she loves for as long as possible.

Sam sketches a simple week for her, and it looks surprisingly modest. It includes brisk walking on most days, two short strength sessions, a little balance practice every day and at least one proper rest day.

People with arthritis, heart conditions, a disability or other long-term illness can also benefit from movement. The plan simply needs to be made with a doctor or physiotherapist who knows their situation.
Sam tells Marta about a woman of eighty-two who joined the gym class at the community hall. A year later she was carrying her own shopping upstairs, and she said she wished she had begun sooner.

Marta's story is meant to encourage and not to treat anyone. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please talk to a doctor or physiotherapist before you change how you exercise.
C1C2: On a warm Saturday, Marta, who was fifty-seven, had spent an hour on the lawn building a tower of blocks with her five-year-old grandson Leo. When lunch was called, she found that she could not get back to her feet without grabbing the arm of a garden chair and hauling herself up with a grunt. Leo did not notice, but Marta did, and the small, unwelcome shock of it stayed with her all afternoon.

Over the garden fence the next morning, Marta confessed her embarrassment to Sam, a retired physiotherapist who had spent forty years helping people move better. He did not laugh or frown, but told her that many people meet this moment somewhere in their fifties or sixties. It was, he said, a message from the body rather than a verdict, and messages can be answered.

Sam drew a gently sloping line on a notepad to show how muscle and strength tend to decline slowly across adult life, often beginning in the middle years. Because the slope is so gradual, he said, most of us fail to notice it until a day arrives when the floor suddenly feels a long way down. The steepness of that slope, however, varies enormously from one person to the next, and it depends heavily on how a person lives.

Age is only part of the explanation, Sam went on, and he tapped his own thigh for emphasis. A great deal of the decline is linked to using our muscles less, as comfortable chairs, cars and screens gradually replace the movement that once filled our days. Researchers find that people who stay active tend to keep far more of their strength than people who do not.

Marta's first fear was that it was already too late, but Sam shook his head and described studies in which people in their eighties and even nineties grew stronger after some weeks of careful training. The body, it seems, keeps its ability to adapt long after youth has gone, and muscles respond to a challenge at almost any age. Progress may be slower than it once was, he admitted, but it is real.

Before any plan began, Sam insisted that she speak to her doctor, especially if she had ever felt chest pain, dizziness or breathlessness, or if she lived with a long-term condition. Marta had no such symptoms, but she booked a check-up anyway, reasoning that it was better to be sure than to be sorry. The doctor gave her a friendly nod and said that, for most people, the greater risk lay in doing too little.

A well-rounded week, Sam explained, draws on four kinds of movement: aerobic activity that raises the heart rate, strength work that challenges the muscles, balance practice that keeps us upright, and gentle stretching. Each of them protects something different, so none of the four can fully replace the others in a sensible plan. The good news was that all of them could be learned in small steps at home.

Sam then quoted the World Health Organization, which advises adults to aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, together with muscle-strengthening exercise on two or more days. It sounded like a mountain to Marta, until he showed her that half an hour on five days would reach it. Anything is better than nothing, he added, and the target is a direction rather than a test.

Marta did not begin with a grand plan, because Sam had warned her that grand plans are the first thing to collapse. Instead she put on her coat after breakfast on Monday and walked once around the block, a journey of about ten minutes. It felt almost too easy, which, Sam assured her later, was exactly the point.

How fast should she walk, Marta wondered, and Sam offered her a simple talk test. At a moderate pace you should still be able to hold a conversation, but you should be too breathless to sing a whole song, and if you can sing easily you could go a little faster. It was a useful rule precisely because it asked her to listen to her own body instead of watching a screen.

Two weeks of daily walking brought no miracle, but Marta noticed subtle changes that she had not expected. She fell asleep more quickly, her afternoons felt less heavy, and she had started to look forward to the moment when she laced up her shoes. It seemed that a body asked to move gently was prepared to repay the favour.

The secret of a habit, Sam suggested, is to attach it to something that already happens every day, such as breakfast or the morning kettle. When one action follows another automatically, you no longer have to argue with yourself about whether to do it, and willpower can be saved for harder moments. Marta put her walking shoes beside the kettle that very evening, and the next morning she followed them out of the door.

Aerobic activity trains the heart, Sam told her, in much the same way that lifting trains an arm. With regular practice the heart can pump more blood with every beat, which means that everyday tasks such as carrying shopping or climbing stairs begin to feel less demanding. Scientists also link regular activity with a lower risk of heart disease, though it is only one of several factors that matter.

Sitting is not a crime, Sam said, but sitting for hours without a break seems to be unkind to the body, even for people who exercise at other times. His advice was disarmingly simple: stand up every half hour or so, stretch, walk to the window or fetch a glass of water. Those little interruptions cost almost nothing and keep the circulation and the joints from stiffening.

Muscles, Sam explained, are not simply for show or for lifting heavy things, because they quietly support almost everything we do. They carry us up the stairs, hold us upright, protect our joints and even help the body to handle the sugar in our blood after a meal. Looking after them is therefore one of the best investments a person can make for the later decades of life.

The first exercise Sam taught was almost insultingly ordinary: sit on a sturdy chair, fold your arms across your chest, stand up slowly, and sit down again with control. It is, he pointed out, the very movement that Marta had failed on the lawn, and practising it strengthens the thighs and hips in exactly the way that real life demands. She managed only five repetitions, and her legs trembled a little, but she finished them all with a grin.

Next came the wall push-up, a gentler cousin of the exercise that frightens people in gyms. Standing at arm's length from the wall, Marta bent her elbows until her nose almost touched the paint and then pushed herself back, feeling her chest and the backs of her arms work. If it became too easy, Sam said, she could simply move her feet further from the wall.

The third exercise was the calf raise, which Marta could perform while the kettle boiled. Resting her fingertips on the counter for safety, she rose slowly onto her toes, paused for a second at the top, and lowered herself with care. Strong calves and ankles, Sam reminded her, are what push us forward with every step we take.

To make the muscles work harder without a gym, Sam handed her a long resistance band that cost about as much as a sandwich. Tins of beans, a bag of rice or a full water bottle, he said, would do the job just as well, because muscles respond to resistance and are not particular about where it comes from. Marta looked at the tins in her kitchen cupboards with new respect, wondering what else in the house might be turned into a weight.

A muscle that is never challenged has no reason to change, so Sam introduced the principle of progressive overload, which simply means asking for a little more as time passes. That might be one extra repetition, a slightly heavier tin or a slower, more careful movement, and it should always feel like a stretch rather than a struggle. Marta began to write her numbers in a notebook and was delighted to see them climb.

Muscles do not grow while they are working, Sam said, but while they repair themselves afterwards, so rest is part of training rather than a break from it. He advised leaving at least a day between hard sessions for the same muscle groups, and filling the gaps with walking or stretching. Marta, who had feared that she was being lazy, was relieved to hear that rest could count as progress.

On the second morning Marta's thighs ached when she climbed the stairs, and she wondered whether she had hurt herself. Sam told her that a dull, mild soreness that appears a day or two after new exercise is common and usually harmless, whereas sharp, sudden or joint pain is a signal to stop and seek advice. Learning the difference, he said, is a skill that improves steadily with practice, and it is one worth having for life.

Quality counts for more than quantity, Sam repeated, and he watched Marta closely as she lowered herself into the chair. Slow, controlled movements work the muscles properly and protect the joints, whereas rushing simply lets momentum do the job for you. He also reminded her to breathe out during the hardest part of each movement and never to hold her breath.

Muscles are built largely from protein, Sam explained, and research suggests that older muscles respond a little less readily to it than younger ones do. For that reason, many people over fifty may do well to eat somewhat more protein than they once did, from sources such as eggs, fish, beans, yoghurt, lentils and lean meat. The exact amount depends on the person, and a dietitian can advise on it.

It seems better to spread protein across the day than to eat most of it at a single dinner, Sam said, because the body can only use so much at one time. Marta decided to add an egg to her breakfast and some beans to her lunch. He added an important warning, which was that anyone with kidney disease should speak to a doctor before raising the protein in their diet.

Marta confided that she would also like to lose a few kilos, and Sam urged her to be cautious. A crash diet can strip away muscle along with fat, leaving a person lighter but weaker, which is exactly the wrong result at this stage of life. Slow, steady changes combined with strength work are far kinder to the body, and a doctor or dietitian can help with a personal plan.

Bones, Sam told her, are not dry sticks but living tissue that is constantly being broken down and rebuilt. With age, and particularly after the menopause in women, the balance can tip towards loss, so that bones become thinner and break more easily, a condition known as osteoporosis. It is common, but it is not inevitable, and there is much that people can do to protect their bones.

Bones respond to stress in much the same way that muscles do, Sam said, becoming denser when they are asked to bear weight. Walking, climbing stairs, dancing and strength exercises all send that useful signal, whereas swimming and cycling, though wonderful for the heart, do less for the skeleton. Marta decided to take the hill route on her morning walk, with a small backpack to make it count.

Calcium is the main building material of bone, Sam said, and it can be found in dairy foods, small fish eaten with their bones, fortified drinks and some leafy greens. Vitamin D, which helps the body absorb calcium, is made in the skin when sunlight touches it, but in darker months or climates some people run short. Whether Marta needed a supplement was a question for her doctor, not for guesswork.

Falls, Sam said gravely, are one of the main threats to independence in later life, and in many countries about one in four people over sixty-five falls at least once a year. A fall can break a bone, and a broken bone can lead to fear and inactivity, which in turn make another fall more likely. The encouraging news is that balance is a skill, and a skill can be trained.

The simplest balance exercise of all is to stand on one leg for as long as you can, with a counter or wall close enough to catch you. Marta began by doing it for ten seconds on each side while she brushed her teeth, and she was alarmed at how much her ankle wobbled. Within a fortnight the wobbling had calmed, and she felt oddly proud of a skill that nobody else would ever notice.

Sam then taught her to walk heel to toe along a strip of tape on the floor, as though crossing a tightrope, with her arms out for balance. He also recommended tai chi, the slow, flowing Chinese exercise, because careful trials suggest that it can reduce falls among older people. Marta, who had always thought tai chi was only for the very calm, signed up for a class in the library hall.

Strength and balance are only half the answer, Sam said, and he walked slowly through Marta's house looking for hazards. A loose rug, a dim staircase, trailing cables and smooth slippers were all accidents waiting for their moment, and every one of them could be fixed in an afternoon. Marta felt a little foolish, but she bought a night light the same day.

Stretching, Sam said, is the quiet fourth member of the family, and the best time for it is when the muscles are already warm. Marta finished each walk by holding a few gentle stretches for about half a minute each, breathing slowly and never bouncing or forcing herself into pain. Her stiff morning shoulders began to loosen, and she found that she could reach the top shelf again.

Marta had put off exercising for years because her knees ached, and she feared that moving would make things worse. Sam explained that, for most people, gentle regular movement helps sore joints, since stronger muscles take some of the load off the joint and movement keeps it supple. He emphasised the word gentle, and said that any joint that was hot, swollen or badly painful needed a doctor.

One cold week her knee flared up, and Marta was tempted to give up altogether, until Sam pointed out that she had other options. Cycling, swimming and water exercise are low-impact activities that keep the heart and muscles working without jarring the joints, and they can fill a gap while a sore spot settles down. She borrowed her neighbour's exercise bike for a month, and the habit survived the sore knee quite comfortably.

Training is only half of the bargain, Sam said, because the body does much of its repair work while we sleep. Most adults need around seven to nine hours a night, and a poor night makes exercise feel heavier and recovery slower, although the effect on any one person varies. Marta resolved to turn off the television an hour earlier and found, to her surprise, that she did not miss it.

It would be dishonest to talk about strength, Sam said, without mentioning smoking, which damages the heart, the lungs and the bones, and which is worth stopping at any age. Heavy drinking is also hard on the muscles, the sleep and the heart, so he suggested that anyone who drinks should keep to modest amounts. These were not lectures, he added, but simply the facts as the evidence shows them.

A friend can do what no plan can, Sam observed, which is to be standing at the gate on a rainy morning when you would rather stay in bed. Marta invited her friend Joy to join her walks, and the two of them found that the miles passed more quickly when they were busy talking. The habit was no longer simply good for her body, because it had become a rendezvous.

Studies repeatedly link strong friendships with better health and long loneliness with poorer health, although it is hard to be certain which causes which. Whatever the mechanism, the effect on Marta's neighbourhood was obvious, because Joy started a Saturday walking group on Beacon Hill and within a month ten people were coming. They finished with tea at the library cafe and talked far more than they walked.

Marta noticed that her mood was brighter on the days when she moved, and Sam confirmed that regular exercise has been shown to lift spirits and ease worry in many people. He was careful to add that it is a helpful ally and not a substitute for professional care, and that anyone who feels low for weeks should talk to a doctor. Exercise opens a door, but sometimes we need a guide to walk through it.

Some research suggests that regular physical activity may help to protect memory and clear thinking as we age, perhaps by improving blood flow to the brain. Sam stressed that the evidence is not yet settled and that nobody can promise any particular result. Since movement brings so many other benefits, however, he saw no reason to wait for a perfect answer before getting started.

In the spring Marta caught a heavy cold that turned into a cough, and for two weeks she did nothing at all. Sam told her not to feel guilty, because every body needs rest at times, but to restart at a lower level and build back up over several days. The setback was not the end of the story, he said, but simply a chapter in it.

Progress is easier to believe in when you can measure it, Sam said, and he showed Marta how to count how many times she could rise from a chair in thirty seconds. Her score had been eight in the spring, and it slowly rose into the teens, which told her more than any bathroom scale could. Walking speed, the ability to climb stairs and simple confidence are also worth watching.

On a warm Saturday in early summer, Marta sat on the lawn with Leo once more, and the blocks went up as high as ever. When lunch was called, she put her feet under her and stood up in a single smooth movement, without a hand on any chair. Leo, of course, did not notice a thing, but Marta did, and she had to blink back tears.

Standing on Beacon Hill with Sam, Marta understood that she had never really wanted bigger muscles. What she wanted was independence, and the freedom to carry her own shopping, travel with friends, climb into a boat and keep up with a grandson who would soon be running faster than she could. Strength, she saw, is simply another name for being able to say yes to the things that make a life worth living.

Sam sketched a simple weekly pattern on the back of an envelope, and it looked surprisingly modest. There were brisk walks on most days, two short strength sessions, a few minutes of balance practice daily and at least one full day of rest. It would not make her an athlete, he said, but it would match what the guidelines recommend, and for most people that is more than enough to begin.

Marta's friend Walter, who lived with arthritis and a heart condition, wondered whether any of this applied to him, and Sam answered carefully. Many people with long-term conditions or disabilities can benefit from suitable movement, he said, but their plan should be designed with a doctor or physiotherapist who knows their situation. Seated exercises, water workouts and gentle walking all have their place, and nobody is too frail to try something.

Sam told Marta about a woman of eighty-two who joined the strength class at the community hall with a walking frame and a sceptical expression. Within a year she was carrying her own shopping up the stairs, and she told the class she only wished she had started thirty years earlier. Nobody can turn back the clock, he said, but almost everyone can improve what the clock has left them.

As the evening settled over the garden, Marta and Sam raised their cups of tea to a year of small steps that had added up to a different life. This book is general information and is not medical advice, and it cannot take the place of a conversation with a doctor or physiotherapist who knows your own health. Whoever you are and wherever you begin, there is a good chance that your body is still willing to learn, so take the first small step today.
